metadata.title: Claude, Icd10 Cm Skill.
metadata.purpose: Take apart the icd10-cm-skill: explain the folder-as-program design, the linear Steps pipeline, and the one-line rule (code only what's documented). Evaluate the trade-off — predictable coding at the expense of any clinical inference — and land the carry-out that coding a diagnosis and making the diagnosis are two different jobs.

beats.narration_text: Feed Claude a clinical note and the setup sounds like a diagnosis is coming. It isn't. icd10-cm-skill takes what a clinician already wrote and re-encodes it as billing codes. Here's the machinery.

beats.narration_text: A skill isn't code — it's a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is icd10-cm-skill: two files, and only SKILL.md carries the instructions. Plain language, no hidden logic underneath. The design choice is severe: the file IS the program, and you can read every line before you trust it.

props.title: A skill is a folder.
props.calloutText: The SKILL.md is the instruction set.

beats.narration_text: The instructions live in a Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and executes it — clinical note in, billable codes out. No branching, no clever inference, unless a step explicitly says so. They optimized for a predictable pipeline at the expense of any freelance reasoning about the patient.

Here's the actual job: turn a clinical note into billable ICD-10-CM codes, the way a professional coder builds the claim. The rule is one line — code only what's already documented. Not a diagnosis, not clinical judgment. Ask Claude to decide what's wrong with the patient and the skill goes silent; that's outside its lane, on purpose. This works if you value a coder who never overreaches; it fails if you were hoping the model would do the doctor's thinking for you.

props.heading: Just what's documented, coded.
props.sparkLine: Not a diagnosis. Just the code.

beats.narration_text: Coding a diagnosis and making the diagnosis are two different jobs — icd10-cm-skill only does the first one.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm wiring an LLM into a medical coding workflow. Take this note — chest pain, shortness of breath, history of hypertension, leg swelling on exam. First, list every diagnosis that's explicitly documented and codeable. Then separately, name what you'd be tempted to infer — like heart failure — that you must not code, because nobody wrote it down. Explain the rule you're using to draw that line. Go deeper: ask the same model to draft the exact query you'd send back to the treating physician to get that inferred diagnosis properly documented, so it becomes codeable on the next pass without any inference on the coder's part.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm wiring an LLM into a medical coding workflow. (1) Explain the difference between diagnosing a patient and coding an already-documented diagnosis, and where the professional line sits between those two jobs. (2) Given this clinical note — chest pain, shortness of breath, history of hypertension, leg swelling on exam — list every diagnosis that is *explicitly documented* and can be coded in ICD-10-CM. (3) Separately, list diagnoses you would be tempted to *infer* from these findings — like heart failure — that must NOT be coded because they are not documented. For each, explain the rule you're using to draw that line.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: draft the exact query the coder should send back to the treating physician to get an inferred diagnosis (say, heart failure) properly documented in the note, so it becomes codeable on the next pass without any inference on the coder's part.
